turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell insisted that a man of his age and position should be able to recall the exact number of his house.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he was quite certain he had given Lady Bracknell the correct number, but he couldn't recall it at the moment.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's voice dripped with disdain as she told Mr. Worthing that this was a most singular and disturbing affair.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he was not accustomed to giving his own social history, and was not sure what further information he could provide.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's voice dripped with disdain as she turned to Gwendolen and Jack, her eyes narrowing in disapproval. She told them that this was a most unfortunate business, and that Mr. Worthing seemed to be a man of considerable mystery, whose family history was far from satisfactory.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell that she was quite certain about her fiancé's character and that she would not be deterred by these baseless accusations.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell turned to Mr. Worthing and asked him to explain the reason for his sudden decision to become engaged to her daughter.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Mr. Worthing explained that he had only recently become engaged to Miss Gwendolen, and that he was not aware of any information about himself that would be relevant to this conversation.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing that she was not satisfied with his vague explanations and that he would have to provide more substantial information about his past if he hoped to marry her daughter.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen insisted that she would not be swayed by her mother's doubts, and that she knew exactly what she was getting into with Jack.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell turned to Mr. Worthing and asked him to provide the name of the estate in which he claims to reside.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack hesitated before asking Lady Bracknell if she would be satisfied with the name of the estate where he stays, rather than the place of his permanent residence.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell turned to Mr. Worthing and asked him to explain the nature of his supposed bachelorhood, to which he had previously referred, and to clarify the status of his supposed engagement to Miss Gwendolen.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack asked Lady Bracknell if she thought it would be possible for him to provide more information about his background in a more relaxed atmosphere, as he felt a bit overwhelmed by the questioning.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing to clarify the discrepancies in his statements regarding his age and the supposed engagement to her daughter, Gwendolen.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack said that he would be happy to provide any further information that Lady Bracknell might require, but he hoped that it would not be necessary to delve too deeply into his family history, as it was a bit of a complicated matter.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that Mr. Worthing's family history was of the utmost importance, and she insisted that he provide her with a full account of his background, including his parents and any other relatives who may be relevant to his suitability as a husband for her daughter.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He hesitated before asking Lady Bracknell if she would consider his profession and character as a suitable replacement for the details of his family history.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's expression turned stern as she told Mr. Worthing that his profession and character, while perhaps satisfactory, were utterly irrelevant to her inquiry into his family background and connections.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he had been quite open about his humble origins and that he did not wish to conceal anything from Lady Bracknell regarding his suitability as a husband for her daughter.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell that she was engaged to Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Gwendolen and Mr. Worthing to pardon her, as they were not engaged to anyone. She explained that when they did become engaged, she or Mr. Worthing's father, if his health permitted, would inform them of the fact. An engagement should come as a surprise to a young girl, and it was hardly a matter she could arrange for herself. While she was making inquiries, Gwendolen would wait for her below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen called out to Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen to wait for her in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen replied to Lady Bracknell that she would wait for her.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing to take a seat.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack stood tall, his eyes locked on Lady Bracknell, and said that he preferred to remain standing, rather than take a seat.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell informed Mr. Worthing that he was not on her list of eligible young men, although she had the same list as the Duchess of Bolton. However, she was willing to enter his name if his answers were satisfactory. She asked him if he smoked.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing admitted to Lady Bracknell that he smoked.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing smoked. She believed that a man should have an occupation. There were too many idle men in London. She asked Mr. Worthing how old he was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he was twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that twenty-nine was a good age to get married. She believed that a man who wanted to get married should know either everything or nothing. She asked Mr. Worthing which category he fell into.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that he knew nothing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing knew nothing. She believed that ignorance was a delicate and exotic fruit that should not be tampered with. She stated that education was unsound and produced no effect in England. If it did, it would be a danger to the upper classes. She asked Mr. Worthing about his income.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his income was between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing if his income came from land or investments.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that his income came from investments.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that Mr. Worthing's income was satisfactory. She stated that land was no longer a profit or pleasure, but rather a means of gaining position and losing it. She asked Mr. Worthing about his country house.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he had a country house with some land, but he did not depend on it for his income. In fact, the poachers were the only ones who made anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing how many bedrooms his country house had. She also asked if he had a town house, as a girl like Gwendolen could not be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he owned a house in Belgrave Square, but it was let by the year to Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing who Lady Bloxham was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack observed that Lady Bracknell went out very little, and that she was a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing what number his house in Belgrave Square was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his house was number 149.
